newsitem.title: UK: Rain benefits UK beet crop, offsets earlier stress.
newsitem.headline: Rain benefits UK beet crop, offsets earlier stress.

text.p: Timely rains have produced a dramatic improvement in the quality of Britain's 1996 sugarbeet crop and higher yields could prompt an upward revision of final sugar output, beet experts said on Monday.
Rainfall on areas with lighter soils in August reduced the drought stress earlier in the campaign and the relatively mild September weather caused an unexpectedly high growth rate.
"The growth rate over the last few weeks, certainly at the end of September, has been double the long-term average," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).

"It's the most growth they've ever seen in September, which is unusual, but some mild conditions are helping that along -- if things carry on this way, British Sugar may revise upwards their estimates on sugar production," she said.

The last of British Sugar's series of field tests, conducted on September 23, showed sugar content at 17.84 percent, compared with 15.80 percent in the equivalent 1995 test and the five-year average of 17.22 percent.
An official at British Sugar declined to comment on output potential, or on numbers of beets sown per hectare, but said the crop was continuing on course for an average result.
"It's done very well, it's benefitted from the rain and the sun," he said.

Czarnikow Sugar recently estimated Britain's 1996/97 sugar output at 1.36 million tonnes raw value, slightly higher than the 1.33 million tonnes turned out in the previous crop year. The area sown to beet has been estimated at 170,000 hectares.
The improved outlook for the crop has resulted in farmers requesting factories to open earlier than the scheduled dates.
While a couple of factories are due to open on Monday, others which had been slated to open on October 3 will now start processing earlier.
"It's nothing that drastic, they've only been tweaked around by a day or so," the British Sugar official said.

But rains are still needed to moisten areas with hard ground such as around York and Newark, although beets in key growing area East Anglia are reported to be ready for processing despite suffering from drought earlier in the growing cycle.
"It's difficult to say at this early stage, obviously things have improved dramatically but still we need some rain," the NFU official said.

"There are hard ground conditions in certain parts of the country where they do need rain...and once the rains have come and gone, the crop should still be large and (sugar) content should still be maintained."
As Britain's mild climate allows for a longer harvest, beet lifting can continue as late as December because there is not as much danger of damaging cold as in some other European nations.
Good weather so far this month has also aided potential.
"It's still relatively warm and the crop has the capacity to grow," said Simon Kerr of the National Institute of Agricultural Botany. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
